questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Childhood: The Foundation Years' refers to.
questions.a: Childhood -- from infancy through early and late childhood -- lays the foundations of all later development: body, language, thought, emotion and social habits. The unit reverses the book's order deliberately: adolescents study childhood to understand their own past and, one day, the children in their care.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Childhood: The Foundation Years'.
questions.a: The years that weigh the least are the years that matter most -- childhood builds the person.

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Principles of Development in Children' refers to.
questions.a: Children's development follows knowable principles: it proceeds in a definite sequence at individual rates, proceeds from head to toe and from centre outward, and grows through the interaction of heredity and environment. Understanding these principles lets caregivers expect, support and not rush each stage.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Principles of Development in Children'.
questions.a: Development has directions and a pace -- predictable in pattern, unique in timing.

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Caregiving and the Child's World' refers to.
questions.a: The unit prepares adolescents for real caregiving: feeding, cleanliness, sleep, safety and play suited to each stage, plus awareness of children's rights and protection needs. Play is treated as the child's serious work -- the medium through which muscles, mind and social skill grow.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Caregiving and the Child's World'.
questions.a: Feed, clean, guard, and above all let play work -- caregiving is supporting the child's own project of growing.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Caregiving and the Child's World' taught, and from which source text?
